paras: The whipping of Henry Meredith was an attack on a Black youth at Armstrong, Missouri, on the night of Saturday, June 13, 1903, when a group of townspeople broke open the city jail, took him out of town and whipped him. Meredith, described as "a negro boy," was being held on a charge of cutting another Black youth, and he was given 150 lashes with a harness tug. The St. Louis Republic presented the attack as the work of citizens who had tired of "disregard for the law," and a short digest of it ran in papers in several states.

Constable Morehead arrested Meredith on Saturday, June 13, on a charge of cutting Will Boggs, who was also described as Black. According to the Mexico Missouri Message, Meredith had badly cut Boggs with a knife after assaulting him "without any cause" and was in jail awaiting trial. Both the Republic and the Message added that he had just finished a term at the State Reform School at Boonville for trying to wreck an Alton passenger train by piling railroad ties on the track.

That Saturday night a body the papers called "a posse of citizens" broke open the jail door and took Meredith out. They took him about half a mile from town, stripped off his outer garments and tied him to a telegraph pole. There he was given 150 lashes with a harness tug. None of the reports names any of the men involved, says how many there were, or describes Meredith's injuries.
No report of arrests of the whippers, of an official inquiry, or of Meredith's trial on the cutting charge appears in the coverage.

The fullest account was a Republic special dated Armstrong, June 14, which ran on June 15 under the headline "Mob Whips a Negro Boy" and the subhead "Armstrong Citizens Tire of Disregard for the Law." A shorter dispatch dated June 15 appeared on June 19 in the Barton County Democrat and the Kinsley Graphic of Kansas under "A Negro Whipped with Harness Tugs." The Mexico Missouri Message ran a version on June 25 headlined "Negro Criminal Whipped by a Posse," calling Meredith "notorious" though he had not yet been tried.

A one-sentence digest item that named no one spread more widely. It said a mob had whipped "a young negro who recently had committed numerous depredations," and first appeared in the Republic's "General Domestic" column on June 15. Over the following days the same sentence ran in the Weekly Corinthian of Corinth, Mississippi, the Daily Ardmoreite and the Newport Weekly Independent. Two Missouri weeklies, the Iron County Register and the Montgomery Tribune, printed it under "Whipped by a Mob" as late as June 25 and 26. No coverage of the attack was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Whipping of Henry Meredith
bases: A 'posse of citizens' or 'mob' broke open the jail, took a Black prisoner out of town and whipped him (A2, A5, A8); no organized whitecap band, threat to kill, or order to leave is reported (A1, A2).

Three differently worded reports (the Republic special A2, the June 15 dispatch A5, and the Mexico Message A8) plus the digest item A1 agree on the jail break and whipping, though all likely derive from Armstrong sources.

accounts.label: Republic special correspondent
accounts.gist: Meredith, arrested for cutting Boggs, was taken from the jail by a posse of citizens, stripped of his outer garments, tied to a telegraph pole and given 150 lashes; the headline presents it as citizens tiring of 'disregard for the law'.

accounts.label: Mexico Message (local Missouri version)
accounts.gist: Calls Meredith 'notorious' and says he had cut Boggs 'without any cause' while awaiting trial; the account of the whipping matches the Republic's.

accounts.label: Wire digest
accounts.gist: A mob broke down the jail door and whipped an unnamed 'young negro' who had 'committed numerous depredations'.

framing.detail: The Republic's subhead 'Armstrong Citizens Tire of Disregard for the Law' and the reform-school background present the whipping as a response to lawlessness.
The Mexico Message headlined 'Negro Criminal Whipped by a Posse' and called Meredith 'notorious', though he was only awaiting trial.
The digest item, run under 'General Domestic', 'Otherwise Unnoticed' and 'Whipped by a Mob', reports the act flatly with the 'numerous depredations' charge.

versions.value: Badly cut William Boggs with a knife, having assaulted him 'without any cause'; 'notorious'

conflicts.note: Not a contradiction about the core event: the reports differ in how far they characterize the charge. All come from the white press; the Republic and the June 15 dispatch state only the charge.
